passage:
Monday. Joseph used to be the first to answer in physics. Today, when Ma'am asked him, he just shrugged. Reena, his sister, noticed he left the dinner table early, his phone face down.
Thursday. Joseph ate lunch alone behind the library. At home, Reena heard him moving around at two in the morning, the light under his door still on. When she knocked, he said, "Go to sleep, I'm fine."
The next Monday. Joseph didn't want to go to school. "Headache." Reena sat on his bed. "You can tell me." He stared at the ceiling. "There's no point. Nobody would believe me anyway." His voice cracked on the last word. Reena didn't leave. She stayed right there.

qa.q: Where did Joseph eat lunch on Thursday?
qa.a: He ate lunch alone behind the library.

qa.q: What does Joseph's line "Nobody would believe me anyway" suggest he feels?
qa.a: He feels isolated and hopeless, believing no one would believe or help him, which hurts even more than the bullying itself.

qa.q: What turning point is available now, and how could Reena use it?
qa.a: Joseph has almost opened up; Reena can stay calm, tell him she believes him and it is not his fault, and help him tell their parents or a school counsellor today. 🤍

qa.q: What is it like for Reena watching her brother over these days?
qa.a: She is likely worried and helpless as she sees him go quiet, lose sleep and say he is fine when he clearly is not.

grounding: It shows a teen boy going silent in class, eating alone, sleeping badly and saying he is fine, believing nobody would believe or help him.

passage: Minakshi, sit with your Sharmila Nani. You asked why I always ask your cousins how school really is. When your Ravi mama was fifteen, he stopped talking at dinner. I thought it was the age. He ate in his room and his light was on until three. When I asked, he said, "I'm fine, Amma." Always fine. I believed him because I wanted to. Months later his friend's mother told me the boys had been cornering him every day, and posting things. I asked Ravi why he never told me. He said, "I thought you'd say ignore them. I thought nobody could help." That sentence still sits in my chest. So I ask, beta. And I listen.

qa.q: Until what time was Ravi's light on?
qa.a: His light was on until three.

qa.q: Why didn't Ravi tell his mother about the bullying?
qa.a: He believed nobody could help and thought she would just say ignore them, so he felt alone with it.

qa.q: What could Sharmila Nani have done differently at that stage?
qa.a: When Ravi withdrew and kept saying "I'm fine," she could have gently kept asking, told him she would believe and help him, and contacted the school.

qa.q: How does Sharmila Nani still feel about that time?
qa.a: She still carries regret; Ravi's words still sit in her chest, which is why she now asks her grandchildren and listens.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage boy withdrawing, eating alone, sleeping badly and saying he is fine, believing no one could help him.
